summary.title: B-trees and database indexes — PlanetScale
summary.one_liner: You learn how B-trees and B+trees work, why databases like InnoDB use them for indexes, and why random keys such as UUIDv4 primary keys hurt insert and range-query performance compared with sequential integers.
keywords: why does uuid slow down inserts
takeaways: A B-tree stores sorted keys in nodes sized to match disk blocks, so lookups visit one node per level and shallow trees are fast.
B+trees keep values only in leaves and link leaves together, letting inner nodes hold more keys and range scans stay in order.
InnoDB stores each table as a B+tree keyed by the primary key, and secondary indexes store the primary key as their value.
Random keys like UUIDv4 scatter inserts across the tree and hurt range queries; sequential integers keep inserts on the right-most path.
Smaller keys such as BIGINT fit more entries per node than 16-byte UUIDs, producing shallower trees.
summary.summary: This interactive PlanetScale article explains B-trees and B+trees, the structures behind indexes in MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB and others. It walks through node ordering, search by levels, block-sized nodes, and how InnoDB stores table data and secondary indexes in B+trees. Embedded visualizations let readers add keys, adjust node sizes and split percentages, and watch insert patterns. It then compares random UUIDv4 keys with sequential auto-increment keys on insert cost, range-query locality, and key size.
